newsitem.title: INDIA: India gas authority calls for LNG supplies.
newsitem.headline: India gas authority calls for LNG supplies.

text.p: State-owned Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL) has made an international call for supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG) as part of a $10 billion project to diversify India's energy needs.

The company, India's biggest distributor and supplier of gas, plans to set up two regasification plants on either coast, each handling at least two million tonnes per year, GAIL Chairman and Managing Director C.R. Prasad said in an interview.
Indian gas demand is expected to leap to 150 million cubic metres per day by 2000 and 200 million by 2005, prompting the country to seek ways to fill the gap.
India's gas production is expected to total only 88 million cubic metres per day by 1997.
A Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas report in August said it favored LNG supplies for southern India, where there was no appreciable gas supply source.
GAIL's Prasad said the company had not started talking to any potential suppliers of LNG yet, but added that he hoped to do so in coming months.
India does not have any facilities to import LNG but, in a bid to encourage development, the government is allowing private companies to import it without a licence.
Energy analyst Wood Mackenzie forecasts India's LNG demand will be about 12 billion cubic metres by 2010.
To help meet part of the demand, Prasad said GAIL plans to form a joint-venture company with state-owned partners Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) and the Indian Oil Corp. (IOC).
He said equity stakes may also be offered to power generators, who will use the LNG.
The companies would take half the shares in the venture, leaving the rest available for public subscription.
"We hope that in the next one year the company may take shape," he said.
But first imports would not occur until 2000 or 2001, he said.

Prasad said the regasification plants would be situated near Madras, on the southern coast, and Mangalore, on the western coast, and each terminal would require around 45 kilometres of pipeline to transfer the gas to nearby power stations.
Prasad was confident that financing would not be a problem.
"We are quite confident of finances...there is a lot of interest to buy because of the demand," Prasad said. He said the partners in the company were also well established.
Potential suppliers of LNG are likely to be Indonesia, whose state-owned firm Pertamina is the world's biggest supplier of LNG.
Several countries that could also potentially serve India's demand are pressing ahead with LNG projects, including Oman, Qatar and Australia.
